1: Pure gambling on the stock market, with stocks pumped through social media, is where this first conversation starts, along with why jumping on hype without research hurts. The hosts also talk through the break cost question around fixed home loan rates of 1.89% to 2.09%, a new accounting app called Thrive, and how a daily coffee habit adds up to about $8,000 a year, before turning to household budgeting.
2: Was JobKeeper there to keep people employed, or did it put a lot of businesses in a better position? Jase, Nick and Marty pick that apart, then look at the claim that only 8% of business owners ever turn over a million dollars. They also cover setting money aside for tax and GST, why lead and lag indicators matter when you chase a goal, and how to think about exiting a business.
3: The world is running out of sand, and Nick explains why that matters for rivers, flooding and construction. From there the hosts look at property prices rising at the fastest rate in almost two decades, why low interest rates are pulling buyers in, what mortgage insurance does and does not protect you from, and how guarantor loans, buyer's advocates and pre-approval change the way people buy.
4: A scam that bought Google ads to catch people hunting for better returns on bonds, then sent their money into crypto accounts where it vanished, kicks this one off. Jase, Nick and Marty go on to talk about forgotten subscriptions quietly draining bank accounts, why it pays to focus on what you're good at instead of chasing every new idea, and what to think about with business plans and business partners.
5: Why are you investing, and over what timeframe? Jase, Nick and Marty start there before explaining NFTs and what non-fungible means, using NBA Top Shots and a digital artwork that sold for $6.5 million. They also cover day trading versus a long-term approach, a negative gearing story where a couple kept accumulating properties, and what $50 a week can grow into over 25 years.
6: Credit cards are not really the problem, the habits around them are. Jase shares his own story of sliding into card debt, while the hosts look at buy now, pay later moving in on digital wallets, why 24% of Afterpay's revenue comes from late fees, and how small facilities can shrink what a couple can borrow, with a $325,000 difference in one example. Dollar cost averaging and offset accounts also come up.
7: What is a business really worth, and when should an owner stop doing the work themselves? Jase, Nick and Marty look at REA's push into mortgage broking and what it could mean for brokers, then ask how a company that has never made money can be valued in the billions, with DoorDash's IPO as the contrast. Nick also shares why he did his own bookkeeping for years and what that habit really cost him.
8: Could you own a slice of a house without having your name on the title? Nick walks through Bricks, which splits a property into 10,000 bricks and borrows only 30% of its value, as one newer way into the market. The hosts also cover the risks of buying property with friends or family, ask whether booming shares and property point to an asset bubble, and talk about why a long term financial plan and a cash buffer matter.
9: Hiring the wrong person is costly, and Marty puts the cost at about 30% of salary, while Nick explains why managing someone out can take 2 to 3 months. The hosts talk about building a team from solo operator to first hires, using personality profiling and culture to attract good people, and why good people refer good people. Jase also covers shares, debt recycling and the Melbourne property market.
10: End of financial year is close, and the hosts start with a simple comparison: one person earning $200K can lose $65,000 to tax, while sharing income across a family looks very different. From there they explain how the immediate asset write-off works on a vehicle, what a super contribution does at a 30 cent tax rate, why a depreciation schedule matters for an investment property, and how a family trust and a bucket company taxed at 26% fit together.
11: The 2021 budget left plenty flying under the radar, and Jase, Nick and Marty ask whether the government is really on the side of everyday Australians. They go through what the ATO is targeting, including work-related expenses, rental deductions, crypto and capital gains, then how tax changes land on mum and dad investors, super for retirees and the Pension Loan Scheme's new no negative equity guarantee.
12: Buying a business after COVID is the main thread here, including why gyms, cafes and restaurants were selling at a discount and what to check before an acquisition, such as whether the owner's knowledge leaves with them. The hosts also cover how sole traders missed out on government support because of their structure, why structure matters before a business has value, and a costly mistake Marty made when he sold his own business.
13: Small amounts put away each day add up over the long term, and a news.com.au article on micro investing gets the hosts talking about habit and compounding. They also work through whether Bitcoin gains are taxable and traceable, why selling within 12 months misses the CGT discount, how pokies and sports betting hook people, and some tools and tips for looking after your mental health.
14: What is it actually like to work with a financial planner, and how does it take the emotion out of money? Nick and Marty share client stories, including people who moved their super into cash after the COVID drop and a client who had 90 days after a property settlement to act. The hosts also touch on Netflix's high performance culture and stress testing repayments at 5%.
15: Insurance is a morbid topic, and Nick's view is that the real mistake is having none at all. The hosts walk through the main types of cover, including life, total permanent disability, income protection and trauma, plus how business partners can protect a shared business. Earlier in the show they weigh up an inheritance tax idea aimed at estates over $3 million and whether a business should start a podcast.
16: A booming share market, a surge in industrial land and a few hard lessons from business owners doing the wrong things. The hosts discuss why 2021 has been so strong for shares, with the Qantas and Woolworths frequent flyer link as one example, why industrial land prices in Melbourne's west are up 20% in eight months, and how a minimum viable product and buying back your own time help a young business grow.
17: Around a million Australians emptied their super accounts through early release, and research found gambling was the second biggest thing that money went on. The hosts talk through what early access can cost, why 22% of surveyed first home buyers used it for a deposit, and BHP weighing up the sale of its petroleum business. A guest from an asset management firm also explains co-investment, listing on the ASX and pre-IPO rounds.
18: Waiting until you need the money is the hardest time to ask for it, and the hosts spend much of this episode on business funding for that reason. They cover separating personal and business debt, director's guarantees, spreading risk across lenders and how commercial lending has loosened. Earlier, Nick takes aim at payroll tax, the state tax that adds a cost to giving people jobs, and the hosts look at margin loans and F45's franchise numbers.
19: Square's takeover of Afterpay, valued at $39 billion and one of the biggest deals in Australian history, opens the show, followed by an ATO warning about tax returns and a Mars themed cryptocurrency that jumped from 11 cents to $2.50 in two hours after a tweet. The main topic is the business plan: why one matters, its seven main elements, weaknesses and threats, monthly cash flow projections, and revisiting the plan every year.
20: Sales gets a bad name, but the hosts reckon it's a fantastic thing when it's done well. Marty talks rapport, solving problems and following through, while Nick covers building lead flow through referral partners and measuring the results. Along the way they look at why Uber Eats leaves restaurants stuck when a delivery goes wrong, the ASX 200 versus S&P 500 headline numbers, and Fred Schebesta's book Go Live.
21: Gig economy side hustles leave a digital trail, and the ATO's data matching from platforms like Uber and Airbnb is the starting point for a chat about not poking the ATO bear. The hosts also look at how small businesses coped through lockdown, why a defensive strategy has to be built before conditions turn, and how that defence becomes offence later. A $260 million crypto hack that was handed back gets a mention too.
22: Why would a lender let a buyer skip mortgage insurance? The hosts explain newer products that swap that big upfront cost for a higher interest rate, and note some lenders now go to 85% on investment loans without it. They also pick over Domain's turnaround after lockdowns, executive pay and long-term incentives, then put Jase in the hot seat on tax, covering capital gains versus capital losses and company structures.
23: Pivot fatigue is real when a business has already changed direction once and the energy for another round is gone. Jase, Nick and Marty talk burnout and Webjet's pivot story, then work through listener questions on paying down credit card debt, getting a home loan after two low income years, the main residence exemption from capital gains tax, and what moving between cryptocurrencies means for tax.
24: Where is the Australian property market heading? A co-founder of 1 Group joins the hosts to cover the COVID move to regional areas, why Brisbane is firing while Melbourne apartments have lagged Sydney, and how flood and climate risk might one day affect loans and values. He also explains why Perth and Adelaide have drawn more caution, and what to look for in boom-area hotspots.
25: Marty opens by comparing household incomes in 1990 with today, which leads into lender caution and interest only loans for owner occupiers. The hosts then cover a brewery's reported sale to Lion, with industry estimates near $500 million, and Clipchamp's acquisition by Microsoft. The second half is about values and culture: how the team set theirs, why leaders must live them, and why values make up 25% of staff reviews.
26: Keeping a small team because they want to be there, not just out of loyalty, is the thread here, as Jase shares how his firm uses software to check in on how staff are feeling and what happened when that data went unread for a couple of months. The hosts also cover alcohol spending and habits, why Elon Musk and Warren Buffett chose simpler lives, and Melbourne selling a year's worth of merchandise in 48 hours after the AFL preliminary final.
27: What does it really cost to process one deal, and where do the best ones come from? Inovayt's general manager explains how measuring leads, referral sources and customer lifetime value shaped decisions, with roughly 150 transactions a month and an operating cost of about $1,200 per deal. The conversation also covers CRM systems, forecasting, and why hiring should be the last fix for an operating problem.
28: How should a business use social media, and does it still need a strong website behind it? A digital marketing specialist joins the hosts to talk about short video, knowing your audience, a consistent tone of voice, scheduling content ahead, and why a team page is often the second most visited page on a site. Earlier, the hosts discuss Marty's take on residential property and how Canva grew into a $40 billion company.
29: Jase and Nick turn the questions on Marty, starting with working in the family milk bar from the age of 7 and running the bread stand there. He talks about teaching Charlie business through coin collecting, his years as a full-time stand-up comedian, and why he thinks he sold his first business too early. He also shares why he believes attitude separates strong business owners from the rest.
30: People who worked from home through lockdown are now being told that flexibility is gone, and that is fuelling the great resignation. The hosts talk through what employers can do about it, then move to how Blockbuster gave way to Netflix and YouTube, and what makes customer service memorable, from the Melbourne Storm's unexpected gesture to Lexus collecting cars for servicing and a property manager who arrives with solutions.
31: At 25, with little business experience but a knack for writing mortgages, Nick went out on his own in 2007. Here the other hosts turn the questions on him, from growing up in a working-class family in regional NSW to the risks of the early days. He talks about the power of saying no, work ethic, setting boundaries and why you cannot over-communicate as a business owner.
32: A business owner's vision often lives only in their head, which leaves the team, and sometimes a partner at home, guessing why everyone is working so hard. The hosts talk about writing a vision on one page, drawing the future on a whiteboard, and the All Blacks one pager with its ambition of winning the 2019 World Cup. Earlier they cover diversifying versus specialising and fixed rates rising by around 0.5 to 0.6 percent.
33: What shapes a business owner? Marty and Nick put the questions to Jase, from growing up playing cricket and years working at McDonald's, to an early accounting job that put him in front of business owners, and then building a new firm from scratch in the middle of the pandemic. It turns personal when he talks about losing his mum, why time can't be bought back, and what he now believes about mental health.
34: A business name that someone else already owns can unravel a brand. Using the Henley Constructions story, a guest from Herbert Smith Freehills explains how trade marks work, the difference between a house brand, a product name and a slogan, and why a free IP Australia search is worth doing before settling on a name. Earlier, the hosts look at F1 team spending under a $145 million cap and why unpaid super is a growing problem.
35: What changed between January and now, personally and in business? The hosts look back on 2021 and ahead to 2022, with takeaways on communication, culture and getting good people around you. Along the way they cover AustralianSuper seeking court approval to set aside member money for regulator fines, why Director ID exists to stop fraudulent director identities, and the great resignation.
36: Fixed rates that jumped by between 1.3% and 1.5% in about three months set the tone here, as the hosts work through inflation, fuel and living costs, and what rising rates could mean for rents and the property market in 2022. They also look at Meta's 26% overnight slump, why Bitcoin and the Nasdaq fell as investors stepped back from risk, and the money behind AFL players, where only 6 earned over $1 million.
37: What does it take to build a business in 2022? The hosts look at record job ads on Seek, the great rehiring, and commercial property as an alternative to residential. They also cover the ATO's expected push on tax debts built up during COVID support, what a Super Bowl ad costs, and why succession planning, knowing your numbers and a clear plan matter as the year gets going.
38: Jase, Nick and Marty explain how a principal place of residence can help you get ahead, including why an offset account matters if the home later becomes a rental, why a valuation at the time of moving out is worth having, and how debt recycling works when borrowing to invest. They also size up a shared equity deposit offer and a new government money website.
39: A sneaker cleaning business built on looking after the shoes you already own sparks a chat about knowing exactly who your customers are. Jase tells a frustrating story about an online shoe order that went wrong and what a good fix would have looked like. The hosts then discuss loyalty rewards that actually suit the customer, referrals, birthday messages, and why a close client relationship helps when things go wrong.
40: Getting into a first home takes more than a deposit, and the hosts walk through what to weigh up, from budget considerations and guarantor loans to understanding your credit file. Before that, they range across the week's headlines, including Elon Musk's challenge to Vladimir Putin, Ford and GM's electric vehicle investments, the federal budget and its beer tax cut, and building costs hitting fixed-price contracts.
41: What should your profit percentage be, and is there one number that fits every business? Jase points to industry benchmarks, including a report on cafes where 91 percent of turnover goes on expenses. The hosts also look at how a South Yarra restaurant pivoted during lockdown, a $2 million fixed price job with a 5 percent margin, and why Marty says to learn to love the numbers.
42: Habits are the thread running through this one. With Jase away, his business partner steps in to run through the 2022 budget, including a $120 deduction for every $100 spent on staff training and technology, before the hosts debate the metaverse and an Uber and taxi partnership in New York. Marty owns up to his weight gain, and the guest explains how a 20 minutes a day running challenge turned into a routine.
43: Tax minimisation is legal and evasion is not, and the hosts spend most of this episode on the first. Nick explains how a deductible super contribution works, up to $27,500 a year, and why fund cutoff dates matter. They also cover fringe benefits tax, the instant asset write-off and its $59,000 cap on passenger vehicles, trust distribution changes and bucket companies, plus Buffett's $144 billion cash pile and Stripe's interest in Australian banking.
44: Why do people hesitate to ask for a pay rise, and what gets in the way? Marty says staff often worry what an employer will think of them, while Nick points out that small business owners rarely have time to plan their people's careers. Marty suggests the habit of exceeding targets, and Jase tells the story of a couple who started the streetwear store Waves from a spare bedroom with their first $5,000 of stock.
45: Telling new hires you do annual pay reviews is easy; having the structure behind it is harder. Jase, Nick and Marty come at career progression and remuneration policy from the business owner's side, including a staff member who left and a team member sitting at 70% of target. Earlier, they ask whether bricks and mortar retail is dying and look at Judo Bank's plan to lift its business lending market share from 1% to 4%.
46: Elon Musk's $44 billion offer for Twitter, about $61 billion Australian, gets a numbers breakdown from Marty, including how the deal is funded and why Twitter's revenue looks small next to Facebook's. Then producer Tommy sits in for Nick to talk with Jase and Marty about turning a passion into a living, and the silver lining that can come from a failed business partnership, drawing on his first media business.
47: Starting a podcast is easy to put off, and the hosts get an inside look at creating podcasts for businesses, from defining what success looks like before you begin to the value of a regular release day. Marty shares that it took about 75 episodes of his own show to gain traction. Jase and Marty also look at rising interest rates, what a rate rise means for a mortgage, and the maths of saving a small amount every week.
48: Crypto's market cap fell from 2.9 trillion to 1.2 trillion, a drop of about 60 percent, and Terra Luna went to nothing in a week. The hosts use that to talk about why investing is not gambling, why diversification and a defensive plan matter, and why understanding the business behind a stock counts. They also look at the $26 billion of JobKeeper that went to businesses whose revenue grew.
49: Customer loyalty, digital marketing and the workplace after COVID are the threads here. Jase looks at an accounting firm that grew through Google search rankings and reviews, reaching $6 million turnover with a team of 9 offshore in the Philippines. Marty brings a damning stat on customer loyalty, and the hosts discuss commissions and team culture, surprising and delighting clients, and why technology needs a human touch.
50: When things look shaky, what can you actually control? Jase and Nick work through the numbers behind the Inspired Unemployed's stake in Better Beer and a grocery delivery start up promising 10 minutes that has raised $86 million, then Remy Capital going into voluntary administration and the ATO chasing debts. They finish on small habits, from keeping the phone off the bedside table to reading a business book with the morning coffee.
52: With the cash rate at 0.85% and another rise expected the next day, the hosts work out what further increases could mean for home loan rates and repayments, using a $1 million loan as the example. They also look at why small businesses worry when customers pull back, a stat that 39% of mortgage holders are concerned, and whether inflation forecast to reach 7% is as high as it gets.
53: Two good staff resigned just weeks after two new hires started, and that story kicks off a debate about the employee market. Jase explains what happened at Future Advisory, Nick argues that anyone leaving for another 5% or 10% can go, and Marty makes the case for getting people back into the office. They compare mandating five days a week with having no rules at all, and what it means for training juniors.
54: Is Australia really one of the riskiest housing markets in the world? Jase reads from an article suggesting a correction of 20% to 30% after Sydney prices rose about 30% over two years, and the hosts weigh it up. Marty argues people simply want to be in homes, Nick points to quality homes and high demand suburbs, and they explain how falling values and heavy borrowing affect banks. Rental affordability comes up too.
55: Is it brave or foolish to buy while everyone is talking about a 20 to 30% drop? The hosts weigh fear against opportunity in 2022, with Marty's example showing a couple's borrowing capacity falling from $1,135,000 at 2.10% to $850,000 at 4.85%, which thins out the competition. Nick explains why some hot areas have already dropped around 10% while the east holds up, and why lenders can differ by $50,000 to $80,000.
56: What happens when you stop chasing the win and start being honest with yourself? Marty talks with a world champion about living authentically, the idea of body, mind and soul, lessons from his father, and losing everything through bankruptcy only to find a better version of life on the other side. They also get into defining your values and why money is not the sole solver of problems.
57: The average first home buyer is now 34.5, and the hosts unpack what has changed since 2000, using a news.com.au article. They cover the idea of 40 year loan terms, the stat that 47% of homeowners aged 55 to 64 still have a home loan against 14% back then, changing attitudes to debt, and being smarter than the system. There is also a fake Indian cricket league built to catch gamblers.
58: A strategic planning day with 28 people in a room, plus teammates in Perth and the Philippines on Zoom, is the story here. Jase explains how the team workshopped its mission and values, sat tables by DiSC personality profile and ran a SWOT. Nick describes his own people-focused planning days, where staff get ten minutes to share something personal, and the hosts talk about culture and why even a team of two or three can run one.
59: What does it take to walk away from a well-paid corporate construction role and back yourself? The guest has worked in construction for over 25 years and recently founded Construction Collaborative. He talks about going from a full income to zero, the sabbatical that gave him time to reflect, working with fund managers on build-to-rent, and the role of resilience, positive visualisation, focus time and creating your own luck.
60: Michelin gave away a guide to restaurants, mechanics and fuel stops in France so that people would want to drive further. Nick uses that story to open a chat about complementary offerings, from cinemas adding Gold Class to a real estate agency running a coffee window. Jase, Nick and Marty then ask what the same thinking could look like in accounting and finance, including annual equity reports and teaching people software.
61: There are ways to fund a business beyond the bank. Jase walks through crowdsourced equity funding, using the ThreadHeads t-shirt company, which drew nearly 7,000 expressions of interest, as his example, and Nick explains why it opens up investments once limited to sophisticated investors. The hosts then turn to Google Trends as a way to test a business idea, including a 3,800% jump in searches for vegan wine.
62: How much room should a bank leave for rates to rise before it lends? The hosts look at the 3% affordability buffer, why Nick expects regulators to trim it when they want lending to move again, and how the UK approaches it. They also explain how living costs are now assessed instead of the old HEM ratio, and why a pre-approval that expires after three months can mean being reassessed at today's higher rates.
63: What does it take to develop people at work the way a coach develops an athlete? Marty runs through 13 steps, starting with setting a clear goal and focusing impact, then releasing the handbrakes holding someone back, finding each person's superpower, and celebrating progress. Nick and Jase share how it plays out in their own teams, from goals on a home screen to finding that too many meetings stood in the way of targets.
64: How does a partner in an accounting firm look after her own health and her team's? A guest from Perth, who trained in accounting and HR, tells the story from a farm childhood and dancing through to partnership, then explains weekly wellbeing surveys for staff, morning breathwork and routines, and why she sees looking out for team health as an employer's responsibility. Becoming a Bikram yoga teacher comes up too.
65: A proposed two year rent freeze leaves Marty and Nick frustrated, arguing it strips landlords of a return just as their costs rise. Nick floats the opposite idea of increasing negative gearing, Jase explains why the NRAS incentive is rarely used by his clients, and the hosts discuss build to rent projects as a private sector answer to the shortage of homes.
66: How do you find a government grant that actually fits your business? Nick tells how a quick application for a $2,000 professional advice grant led him to a $5,000 ventilation grant, and Jase shows how searching business.gov.au turned up 679 grants and programs, with up to 208 he could be eligible for. They also cover hiring JobSeeker, upskilling staff, mental health coaching and digital tools grants.
67: Australian businesses are struggling to find skilled people, and the hosts look at why. Migration dropped 71 percent in 2021, and about half of accountants were born overseas compared with roughly 30 percent of all employed people. They discuss training up unskilled hires, keeping older workers on part time, the idea of lowering the working age to 13, building offshore teams in the Philippines and elsewhere, and whether the four day week trial stacks up.
68: With interest rates and costs climbing, the hosts look at how households and small businesses can stay ahead. They talk about why tighter budgets matter, how a lower loan to value ratio tends to bring a better rate, why a mortgage set up two years ago deserves another look, and how a small rate difference adds up over five to seven years. Jase also reports back from XeroCon.
69: Being the AFL's number one draft pick and a premiership player did not protect a young footballer from depression and anxiety, and he explains why he walked away from the game in 2019. He tells Jase and Marty about the pressure of a record $7 million contract, why he kept struggling alone, and the writing that gave him purpose. They also discuss accounting firm burnout and what fatherhood has changed.
70: Roger Federer's off-court business smarts kick off a chat about building income beyond your day job. Marty tells the story of a client on a government salary who used subdividable investment properties and a clear plan to reach $200,000 from her investment strategy, while the hosts discuss side businesses, extra revenue streams, employee shares and why super is often the biggest asset people have.
71: The ATO is chasing around $60 billion in tax debt, and the way it collects has changed. Marty and Jase explain why interest on an ATO payment plan now sits at 9.31%, how a two year plan can squeeze cash flow, and what happens when major lenders will not fund a tax debt. They walk through short term lenders, moving to commercial funding later, and the options if the debt cannot be repaid, including liquidation or voluntary administration.
72: One day an article says property investors are staying away, the next day another in the same newspaper says they are back. Nick uses that confusion to work through seven things to check before buying after a price drop, including how far prices have really fallen in that suburb, what a 6% interest rate does to cash flow, and what drives an area, such as demographics, infrastructure and council plans.
73: Plenty of business owners don't even have employment contracts for their staff, and Nick explains the moment the penny dropped for him: when he was getting ready to manage someone out of the business. The hosts discuss using an external HR group for contracts, pay templates and casual and part-time rates, building a clear career pathway, an employee value proposition, and 30, 60 and 90 day check-ins for new starters. Jase shares his team growing from 14 to 28.
74: After the Optus and Medibank data breaches, the hosts ask what cyber crime really costs a business. They cover how an open API and compromised credentials were involved, Medibank's share price falling 20%, the average business cost of $276,323 quoted from infrastructure.gov.au, phishing tests on staff, cyber insurance, and a client email hack that let a scammer pose as a conveyancer.
75: A healthy profit and a nearly empty bank account can happen at the same time, and Jase explains how. He works through profit versus cash flow, accruals versus cash basis, and why a P&L and a BAS can show different figures. Aged receivables, loan repayments and stock balances all come into it, while Nick covers good debt versus bad debt and Marty talks about knowing the rhythm of your business.
76: Electric cars used to mean Tesla and little else, but Nick has noticed more brands on the road lately, and Jase says clients now ask about them almost weekly. All three hosts say their next car will probably be electric. The conversation then turns to car makers selling features like heated seats and steering wheels as app subscriptions, and what that could mean for new buyers, resale and manufacturing.
77: Fighting a crowded market for the same customers is the red ocean, and Marty explains the alternative: Blue Ocean Strategy, which is about creating uncontested market space and making competition irrelevant. He covers breaking the usual trade off between value and cost, and how an existing business could apply the idea to differentiate its service. The chat opens with the hosts reflecting on turning 40 and 50.
78: What actually pushes prices up, and how do you raise your own without losing clients? Jase explains inflation through increased money supply, devaluation and cost-push, then the hosts talk communication, context and clarity when lifting prices. Shrinkflation gets a run, from Doritos bags losing five chips to a snack company's gas bill going from $3 million to $9 million a year, plus Marty's toilet paper news.
79: After the Medibank and Optus hacks, the hosts get practical about protecting your identity and your money. Nick explains how a credit reporting agency can stop anyone opening credit in your name, how a fake conveyancer email sent a settlement of about $800,000 to a scammer, and why a quick phone call to confirm account details matters. Password phrases, two-step logins and a scam phone call also come up.
80: Is paying land tax instead of stamp duty a smarter way into a first home? Nick works through a million dollar purchase, with stamp duty around 5% set against an annual land tax of $400 plus 0.3% of the land value, and the hosts weigh the arguments on both sides, including the risk that prices rise. Jase then raises how Australia compares with the rest of the world when it comes to GST.
81: Humility as a business strategy is the idea here. Marty tells the Toyota story: how it studied American carmakers like Ford, blended what worked with its own strengths, and aimed to be a cost leader without compromising quality, with humility as its number one corporate value. Nick and Jase pick up continuous improvement and why a business needs it spoken about from the leaders down to everyone.
82: Selling the business you built can feel like a loss, not a win. A founder who sold her software company to an ASX listed firm talks about the heartbreak of that sale, a negotiation that was not the smooth sailing she expected, and why she never sees herself retiring. The conversation also covers getting electronic signatures accepted in Australia, identity verification, and how small firms can think about scams and hacks.
83: A one page strategy, set out as what you want to achieve, why, and how you will get there, is the centrepiece here. With Marty and Jason away, Nick talks with a guest who has 35 years in senior leadership across financial services and building, covering his time at the Commonwealth Bank's private bank, starting his own consulting business, the value of networking, and how an advisory board keeps people accountable.
84: Qatar's reported spend on the World Cup was $300 billion, and Jase, Nick and Marty ask who actually comes out ahead. They look at the $45 billion spent building the city of Lusail, the $7.5 billion FIFA pocketed against the prize money for the teams, and the flow-on from Messi and Mbappe merchandise. They then turn to the summer's potato shortage and what it means for restaurants weighing up higher chip costs.
85: Interest rates rising eight times in 2022 taught Marty to keep asking where you can get ahead when the market turns cautious. Nick talks about getting comfortable with being uncomfortable as a business grows, and Jase explains why quality beat quantity for his team. The hosts then trade light-hearted predictions for 2023, including Bob Iger's return to Disney, the rise of AI and Essendon's finals hopes.
86: ChatGPT became the fastest app in history to reach 100 million monthly users, and Jase uses that as the starting point to explain what it is, why OpenAI was created and who backs it. The hosts look at how fast AI tools are multiplying, from 849 to 901 in a week, and Jase's experiment where a tool drafted a 732-word blog article in 34 seconds.
87: Recession talk and rising interest rates can have business owners reacting before anything has happened to them. Nick, Jase and Marty argue for understanding the trends without letting them run the business, with examples such as an electrical firm moving into electric vehicle charging installations and commercial fit-outs aimed at the medical space. They also cover adding complementary revenue streams and having a defensive plan for expenses.
88: A recession is two quarters of negative growth, but Marty says the psychology around it is what really concerns him. He talks through who is most exposed, why standing out and doing the work others won't counts in a slowdown, and which industries tend to be hit, including real estate, construction and hospitality. Jase shows how the same supermarket basket quietly costs more, and Nick explains reversing the budget.
89: A third of the home loan market is coming off fixed rates within 12 months, yet AFG data showed the lowest take up of fixed loans in a decade. The hosts compare variable rates near 5% with fixed rates closer to 6%, why banks have already priced in rate rises, and why 2% fixed rates may never return. They talk through the barbecue question of staying variable or refixing, and what paying down debt can do.
90: What if tax simply happened in the background, with no return or BAS to lodge? Jase explains the ATO's push towards a fully digital system by 2030, including real time collection of GST, which would end payment plans because the money leaves your account as it is owed. Nick and Marty react to growing small business tax debt, and Nick floats simply taking 25% of revenue.
91: Why is the office still worth turning up to? Marty opens with the 41% of people who reported isolation and mental health struggles during lockdowns, and the hosts argue that collaboration, friendships and learning from colleagues are easy to underrate. Nick talks about young staff missing out on mentors and phone skills, while Jase describes how working from home stretches his hours and blurs his routine.
92: Seven ways to wreck a business, drawn from about seven years of business banking, are Marty's topic this week. He covers losing focus, avoiding price rises, failing to delegate, ignoring the numbers and expecting people to read your mind, while Jase and Nick share their own experience of running a business, including a leadership course note that leaders don't get to show bad days to the team.
93: Phones and social media are changing how we communicate, and Nick, Jase and Marty unpack what that means for friendships, the way we take in news, work and sleep. They talk about cyberbullying, algorithm-tailored feeds and getting lost scrolling, then finish with practical ideas for taking back control, like reviewing your screen habits, turning off notifications and building up no-go zones.
94: A family trust can distribute profit to adult children before 30 June, but what if the money never actually reaches them? Jase explains Section 100A, the ATO's anti-avoidance rule, including unpaid entitlements, reimbursement agreements, bucket companies and the fact that the changes reach back to 2014. He also covers the ATO's green zone and red zone guidance, why paperwork matters, and why starting tax planning early helps.
95: How does a newcomer take on established mattress retailers? The hosts study Koala as a case study: unique foam technology, a queen-size mattress light enough to carry by hand, delivery to the door within about 4 hours in Melbourne and Sydney, and 39,000 5-star reviews. They also look at $100 million in net revenue in 2020, a 48% jump, and what business owners can take from finding an angle to dominate.
96: A swimwear brand that took off after Kendall Jenner posted about it looks like a rags to riches story from the outside, but what did the success cost on the inside? Nick brings the founder's story, and the hosts talk about the collateral damage of running a business 24/7 and building balance in no matter how busy it gets. Jase also draws on The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari, including living with discipline and embracing the present moment.
97: Shoes of Prey began in 2009 with a simple idea, custom-designed shoes, grew to 200 staff and raised more than $30 million, then fell. Marty shares the case study and the hosts pick at why: decision fatigue at checkout, heavy fixed costs, a $100 million revenue target, market research that said one thing while shoppers did another, and buyers wanting what influencers wear instead of designing their own.
98: A 30% tax on super balances over $3 million was announced, and the hosts ask who it really reaches. Nick covers the Financial Services Council's estimate that 500,000 Australians could be caught, the lack of indexing and the $2 billion expected in the first full year, and why taxing unrealised gains could force funds to sell property. They also discuss ripple effects on the family home and on money moving into companies.
99: Berkshire Hathaway was up 4.1% in 2022 while the S&P 500 fell 18.1%, and Marty uses that and the annual letter to talk about patience, value and holding for the long term. The hosts pull out lessons on buying good businesses with strong cash flows, investing in people, keeping cash on hand, and the CEO as risk officer. Marty is clear it is a look at a letter, not investment advice.
100: Most podcasts stop after about 7 or 8 episodes, so reaching 100 gave the hosts plenty to reflect on. Jase, Nick and Marty look back on the cost and time of showing up every week, why purpose keeps you going and how it got easier. They tie it to business through the flywheel effect from Jim Collins, consistency in how you treat clients, adaptability, resilience and learning from setbacks.
101: When is it time to worry about a business? Jase, Nick and Marty work through the warning signs: sales drying up, fewer word of mouth referrals, clients choosing to go elsewhere, and cash flow stress that leaves tax unpaid. They also explain what can happen when it goes further, from a small business restructure to liquidation, and what that means for being a company director again.
102: Bunnings is moving into pet food and toys, and the hosts ask what that means for specialist pet stores. After a few pet stories from Jase and Marty, they cover the jump from a couple of hundred pet products to 1,000, why an add-on at a store people already visit on weekends makes sense, and what Pet Barn might make of it. The lesson they take is to separate a genuine complementary offer from a distraction.
103: A letter from a local real estate agent warning homeowners about loans moving from fixed to variable rates has Nick fired up, and it leads into a chat about crisis and opportunity. Marty and Jase look at insolvencies running well above usual, why a business in a position of strength might consider an acquisition, how payment proposals can help a business with ATO debt, and why culture and due diligence matter when buying.
104: Money worries follow people to work, and Nick shares a Canadian study finding that financially unwell employees spent about a third of their work time worrying about money and were 16% less likely to engage. The hosts talk through what financial wellbeing seminars cover, from budgeting and emergency funds to getting into property, why so many people lack the basics, and what employers can do, including apps.
105: The 2023 federal budget, read through a small business lens. Jase walks Nick and Marty through the $500 electricity bill relief for people on certain concession cards, the $20,000 instant asset write-off limit, the move to paying super in real time from 1 July 2026, and an amnesty on failure to lodge penalties for small businesses behind on their tax. They also talk through payroll cycles and end of year planning.
106: Some businesses are flying while others are struggling, and the hosts say that gap is why owners need to get real with their numbers. After 11 interest rate rises in 13 months, they cover why not to go all in on growth, learning to read a profit and loss and balance sheet, budgeting and forecasting, setting cash aside for tax, and getting on top of debt such as a growing ATO balance before it's too late.
107: What does the chief executive of a billion dollar company say about getting ahead? Marty shares career advice from Andrew Reeves of Inghams, starting with doing the job you are in as well as you possibly can. Jase, Nick and Marty talk about surrounding yourself with people who challenge you, how younger staff think about growth paths, and why continuous learning and accountability matter in leadership.
108: Two incomes of $90,000 each feel comfortable until one stops for a baby. Marty runs the numbers on upsizing before starting a family: a $900,000 purchase with $55,000 stamp duty, then living costs of $5,700 and repayments of $4,400 a month, leaving a $4,393 monthly shortfall on one wage. Nick explains why he leans towards rentvesting, and the hosts talk about building a savings buffer.
109: What if measuring success only in money leaves out everything else? A coach who came from wealth advisory explains the four pillars he built after clients told him success was a narrow term: nutrition, movement, mindset and environment. Marty and Nick share their own struggles with balance and sleep, and the conversation covers accountability, getting clear on an end goal, and how your workspace and the people around you shape resilience.
110: Victoria's budget plans to abolish upfront stamp duty on commercial property and replace it with a 1% land tax on the unimproved land value over ten years. Marty runs the numbers on a $1.2 million land value costing $12,000 a year, Nick warns industrial tenants usually pay outgoings so rents may rise, and the hosts also cover land tax reaching 380,000 more homes and banks easing serviceability buffers.
111: Money has little to do with how smart you are and a lot to do with how you behave. Jase, Nick and Marty work through the first batch of lessons from Morgan Housel's The Psychology of Money, including why no one is crazy with money, why a sense of enough matters, how compounding works, tails you win, luck and risk, and the idea that wealth is what you don't see.
112: Saving money today so compounding can work later is the first of the remaining lessons from Morgan Housel's The Psychology of Money that the hosts run through in part two. They cover leaving room for error, the difference between being rational and being reasonable, why past surprises are a poor guide to the future, taking cues from people playing a different game, how your own goals change, and the pull of a good story.
113: Home ownership is slipping down Australians' list of financial priorities, with 55% naming financial independence as their number one. Marty shares the report and its definition of financial freedom as passive income covering daily expenses. Nick and Jase talk through why younger people may be shifting, from costly property and higher interest rates to the lasting effects of COVID, and the dream lifestyle versus dream home trade-off.
114: Why does Australia struggle with productivity, and what has that got to do with inflation? Nick explains output for hours worked and runs through the factors, from easy tasks going offshore and regulation to monopolies and zombie businesses that can only just meet their debts. Jase and Marty add the slow uptake of technology, its cost for small business, and an ageing population where 25% of Australians will be over 65 by 2043.
115: Is Australia's tax system holding people back? Jase makes the case for taxing consumption more and income less, using a big spender buying a flash car as the example, while the hosts question why tax rates slide up with income. He also explains how Ireland drew in Facebook and Google with effective rates between 2% and 4.5%, and how a global minimum tax of 15%, backed by 136 countries, aims to close that gap.
116: Ange Postecoglou's coaching career gives Marty a set of lessons that work just as well in business. He covers Ange's lifelong study of the game, holding both the individual and the team accountable, and communicating with everyone from the players to the people who look after the boots and the kit. Nick and Jase tie each lesson back to team culture and what it takes to lead a business.
117: Kelly Partners has acquired 83 accounting firms over 17 years, and Jase uses it to ask whether he would be better buying a business or growing organically. The hosts look at its 32% yearly growth, ASX listing and the valuation multiples involved, then weigh pros such as immediate operations and easier finance against cons like cost, culture fit and change management, drawing on Nick's experience of acquiring.
118: Nine out of ten rental property tax returns the ATO goes through are reported incorrectly, according to the numbers Jase shares, which is why rental owners sit near the top of its firing line. He and the hosts go through common slips: holiday homes used by the family, redrawn loan money spent on a car while the interest is still claimed, repairs that are really capital improvements, and Airbnb stays with thin records. They also cover personal returns, where the ATO expects close to half a billion in extra receipts.
119: Rising interest rates and weaker demand for holiday rentals are squeezing Australian property investors. Marty runs the numbers on a $750,000 investment property rented at $600 a week to show how cash flow has shifted, Nick explains why many investors cannot afford to keep holding, and Jase describes clients selling. They also cover capital gains planning before a sale and the 800,000 fixed loans coming to an end.
120: Record profits are landing while households feel the squeeze, and Nick singles out Coles, Woolworths and Qantas. He points to a Qantas record profit on track for $2.48 billion and Coles profit up 17.1% on sales up 4.1%. Jase shares his frustrations flying Qantas, and Marty suggests consumers vote with their feet by supporting small business and local farmers markets.
121: You only need to win about 51 percent of the room, and not everyone will like you. That is one of eight lessons Marty took from his days as a stand-up comedian at 17 or 18, and he applies them to leadership and business. He talks about laughing at mistakes, resilience, reading the room in real time, using humour to calm someone who is overwhelmed, and facing anxiety with courage. Nick and Jase add their own takes.
122: Threads had only just launched, and Marty reckons Zuckerberg played it cleverly: no ads, 500-character posts, video, an easy sign-up through Instagram, though no direct messages yet and cancelling means giving up Instagram too. The hosts weigh what it could mean for Twitter and the Musk and Zuckerberg cage fight talk, then revisit a notorious marketing misfire, the Pepsi campaign that offered a Harrier jet for Pepsi points.
123: Household savings are running thin while costs and mortgage repayments keep climbing. Jase, Nick and Marty look at a savings rate that fell to 3.7%, the lowest in 10 years, after peaking around 24%, and what that leaves someone on $80,000 when the car breaks down. They also talk about treating the household like a business, reviewing a mortgage rate, and how business owners are going in the first full year without government support.
124: What can a business learn from an AFL club? Marty reports back from a Collingwood Football Club leadership event with five lessons: know your core business, look at yourself first when something goes wrong, water what you want to grow, value different opinions in your leadership group, and learn from mistakes. Jase and Nick react to each one with examples from how they run their own businesses.
125: How much can AI do for a small business today? Jase shares what he uses, mainly ChatGPT and Google Bard, and explains why being specific about your country, state and job gets a better answer, with a business plan request for a team of 28 as the example. Nick talks about building a data lake and doing more volume with the same staff, and Marty likes it for social media content.
126: Why do so many of us stop learning new things as we get older? After watching a documentary on Jake Paul, Nick talks about how taking up golf and swimming later in life brought resilience, plateaus and breakthrough moments. Marty shares his 40/40 challenge of learning drawing for 40 minutes a day for 40 days, and the hosts discuss cognitive reserve, a richer identity and the pull of building a skill.
127: Smaller refunds are catching people off guard, and Jase explains why: the Low Middle Income Tax Offset has been removed, which for a couple could mean about $3,000 less back. The episode busts myths on whether earning more means losing half your pay to tax, covers the changes to what the 52-cent home office method includes, and explains why an accountant can only do so much without receipts and a logbook.
128: What drives a business to succeed: belief, passion or just a good idea? Marty tells the story of his son Charlie's coin business, where selling 7 coins to one customer brought in about $120 and $51 profit, and asks what that says about loving your work. The hosts then compare WeWork, whose valuation fell from $47 billion to $10 billion, with the Zimmermann fashion brand.
129: Strong demand, low supply and rising interest rates are squeezing the property market, and Nick explains why prices are holding up. He covers cash buyers who aren't affected by rates, owners who can't get the borrowing they once did, and the high cost of building new homes. The hosts also look at Victorian policy, including the windfall tax, the idea of capping rents, and why investors are selling.
130: What does your A-game look like, and what trips you into your B-game? Jase recaps the top four steps from high-performance mindset coach Emma Murray's Xerocon talk, including catching negative thoughts, controlling your morning, a deep breathing technique and a 21 day habit stacking cycle. Marty and Nick share how they reframe stress. The episode also starts with Nick on Adelaide missing the AFL finals and the review system behind it.
131: Small businesses are the heart and soul of the Australian economy, yet the Small Business Matters report points to real pressure. The hosts discuss higher borrowing costs for expanding, the struggle to turn a profit and fewer young Australians keen to start a business. Nick explains how interest now factors into acquisitions, and Jase brings in Xero's Small Business Insights, compiled from 3.7 million subscribers.
132: A real estate leader who has spent 20 years with one company, and the last decade running it, talks through how he leads. The managing director of Barry Plant Eastern Group tells Jase and Marty how the property market is loosening after tight stock, why people skills still beat a text message, how top performers win the morning, and how training suits each stage of an agent's career. He also covers moving from salesperson to leader.
133: Being clever on paper and being smart in life are not the same thing. Marty brings an idea from Morgan Housel on intelligence versus smarts, and the hosts talk about EQ, why an accountant can be great with numbers but struggle to connect with people, and how confidence, boundaries and metrics help people perform. It opens with how screens have stolen our attention and why letting your mind wander matters.
134: Can you retire from work and still live well to 100? Nick unpacks the Netflix documentary Live to 100: Secrets of the Blue Zones, including Sardinia and Okinawa, where diets are mostly whole plant foods and exercise is built into the day. The hosts talk about how those habits might fit a busy modern life, and whether a hard line between working and retired is the right idea at all.
135: Plenty of people are buying small businesses that make losses, which Marty finds disturbing. He lays out 12 questions to ask before buying, starting with whether the industry is emerging, steady or declining, whether revenue and profit margins are rising or falling, what the current owner plans to do next, and whether customers are loyal to the business rather than the owner. Jase shares a sale that went wrong.
136: Uber made a quarterly global profit of $394 million for the first time, after a $2.6 billion loss the year before, and Nick uses it to ask what happens when growth businesses are pushed to chase profit. With a higher cost of capital, he says, it is no longer growth at all costs. The hosts also look at Uber's move into flights and travel bookings, and Marty's view that one great product builds the trust to sell more, with Koala Mattresses as an example.
137: Where do you draw the line on cheating? A story about runners in a Mexico City marathon who reportedly used vehicles or public transport to cut the course leads Marty to ask what happens when you don't set your own standards of integrity. The hosts connect it to cheating culture in the Tour de France, accountants questioning odd tax return claims, and a gas leak scam involving a $5,200 quote at Jase's dad's house.
138: Where have all the accountants gone? In the season finale, Jase breaks down the accountant shortage in Australia, from burnout and constant regulation changes to fee increases that haven't kept pace with the work. With Nick and Marty, he talks about accountants as financial storytellers, moving from tax return to trusted advisor, and what it would take to get the next generation interested in the profession.
139: Adrian Portelli went from The Block to LMCT+, a business with turnover of more than $70 million built on memberships, partner brand discounts and prize giveaways. The hosts unpack how the model makes its money, why it is classed as a trade promotion, how social proof and FOMO keep people subscribed, and the gambling regulator investigations that Jase says have so far cleared it. Marty and Nick weigh in on its simplicity.
140: Valuations get the accountant in Jase excited, so the hosts start with Russell Crowe's investment in the South Sydney Rabbitohs and ask how sports clubs actually make money. They run through five common revenue streams, tickets, merchandise, broadcasting rights, sponsorships and marketing, then look at NFL broadcasting deals, Premier League wages, NBA salaries, and how streaming and online betting are changing the business of sport.
141: Small business registrations in Australia keep climbing despite 14 rate rises and a cost of living squeeze. Marty, Nick and Jase look at the jump in new registrations, why young people and women are starting out, and how access to platforms and freelance work has changed attitudes to being your own boss. They also cover the high shutdown rate, ABN pitfalls for contractors, and Xero data showing sales up 5.5 percent year on year.
142: Why haven't rising rates tamed inflation yet? The hosts walk through how the Reserve Bank uses interest rates, why baby boomers earning more on their savings may be keeping spending up, and why an 8.5% to 9% serviceability test leaves many borrowers unable to get approved. They also cover developers with no margin, unemployment heading into 2024, and getting business cash flow sorted before a tight December and January.
143: Should pay depend on how often you are in the office? Nick starts with Origin Energy and Suncorp linking office attendance to bonuses, and the hosts compare notes. Jase's team has a guideline of at least half the week in the office, while Marty says the business owners he speaks with lean closer to 80/20. They also cover results versus presence, visibility, whether remote staff could be paid less, and how juniors develop.
144: Charlie Munger gets a tribute from Marty, who takes concepts from a book on his thinking and applies them to everyday business and life. The hosts talk about adapting before you are forced to, why a victim mentality hurts, acting on problems early, and buying a great company at a fair price over an average one at a great price. Marty also works through how yearly tax changes the compounding of $100,000 over 30 years.
145: Ryan Richardson built Dashboard Insights to fix his own problem: after more than 17 years as an accountant, he felt like a slave to the business and wanted decisions backed by real data. He tells how the tool grew from an internal fix into a product when other firms asked for it, how TNM Consulting works with clients, why offshoring through SYNCT leans on retention, and where AI fits, with a recycling business as a case study.
146: Black Friday sales are now about 20% larger than Boxing Day sales, and 10 million people reached for their credit cards, which Marty says is 14% up on last year. The hosts talk through what that means for spending habits, whether a sale actually saves you money, and how to build a budget with a savings ratio that suits you, with savings leaving your account first so you don't spend the money you can see.
147: Early access to super is a last resort, and Nick explains the narrow ways to release it before retirement, including compassionate grounds when a home is at risk, financial hardship after 26 weeks on government support, terminal illness and IVF, plus the tax consequences. The hosts weigh up what the money could grow to by retirement, and talk about contacting lenders and the ATO early.
148: At 16 or 17 you are asked what you want to do for the rest of your life, and the hosts ask whether university is still the best answer. Jase did an accounting degree without learning what a BAS was, Nick left uni to work in mortgage broking, and Marty says the kids in his family are working by 15. They compare theory with on-the-job learning, trades, HECS debt and the stigma around who goes to uni.
149: Most owners fall into business because they are good at what they do, then hit a tipping point where the wheels can fall off. Marty brings a list on scaling, and the hosts talk through recognising growth barriers, the edge small businesses have over bureaucratic big ones, stretch goals, advice from seasoned owners, hiring great salespeople, streamlining processes and building a budget and forecast for expansion.
151: How do busy CEOs protect time for real work? Marty and Nick bring a list of habits from nine CEOs, including a meeting free day each week, shorter 20 minute meetings, a fake commute for uninterrupted thinking, and sending fewer emails to receive fewer. Jase and the others test each idea against their own routines, from ditch, delay or delegate on the to do list to deleting social media apps and learning to say no.
152: The revised stage three tax cuts shift the benefit down the income ladder. Jase explains that the biggest bracket now gets about $4,500 instead of $9,075, while someone on $60,000 goes from $375 to $1,179 better off, and that the change is expected to save the government a billion dollars over four years. The hosts also debate tax reform, what it means for tax planning, and the difference between marginal and effective rates.
153: Cash use in Australia has dropped by about 60% since 2007, and the hosts ask what that changes. Nick shares economist Stephen Koukoulas's view on the old cash economy and how many more transactions are now recorded. They discuss what that means for tax and inflation, what card merchant fees do to a $50 note, how different generations use cash, and how to budget when every purchase is a tap.
154: Franchise or investment property? Marty shares a client facing exactly that choice and how three questions shaped it: where are you at, where do you want to go, and what is important to you. The hosts discuss linking a goal to the gap and a plan, matching a move to your skills and your time, and making fewer but better decisions.
155: Small settings in software people already use can save hours, and Jase shows how: automating bank transfers in Xero, building custom reports, setting invoice reminders and comparing budget to actual. The hosts talk about Hubdoc for receipts, Podium's AI that drafts replies to Google reviews, and why new tools stall when staff default to the old way. Nick explains how large a tech stack a mix of finance services needs.
156: Dale Carnegie's book How to Win Friends and Influence People, first published in 1936, supplies the leadership ideas as Nick walks the group through its principles on feedback: begin with praise, raise mistakes indirectly, talk about your own mistakes first, let people save face, praise every improvement and give someone a fine reputation to live up to. Jase and Marty share how these play out with their teams.
157: What does it cost to get into a Super Bowl, and who profits from the tickets? Nick unpacks a nosebleed seat at US$950, a box at US$1.2 million, the resale market, and how On Location is allocated 11,000 NFL tickets a year. The hosts compare that with Australian ticketing, dynamic pricing and AFL grand final demand, and Marty tells the story of snagging a corporate box.
158: A coffee at Dead Man Espresso in South Melbourne is where Jase and Nick first met, and it kicks off a chat about how good business relationships and referral partnerships form. The hosts cover what makes a partner worth working with, shared values, making sure both sides win, finding time to meet new people, and why setting documented targets on lead flow keeps a partnership accountable.
159: From a $1.4 billion valuation to about $114 million, F45's slide is the case study. Jase traces how a 45 minute high intensity workout that began in Paddington, Sydney grew to over 2,200 franchises across 60 countries, then looks at oversaturation, competition, COVID and the risks of rapid franchising. The hosts also cover how franchise fees shape growth and what to check before signing a franchise agreement.
160: How does a $180 million tax fraud happen, and why does the ATO seem to chase small debts while big ones slip through? Nick walks through a case of companies sunk with unpaid PAYG withholding. Jase explains phoenixing and director ID, and shares a client who arrived with 18 shopping bags of records covering 18 years. They also cover the TikTok GST refund fraud and why agencies struggle to join the dots.
161: Could homeschooling produce the business owners and professionals of the future? Marty explains why he moved his son out of mainstream school after bullies and trouble concentrating in a crowded classroom, how two hours a day of direct education plus real-life learning like cooking now works at home, and why he is questioning a return. Nick pushes back on the social side and schoolyard resilience, and a 19% rise in Victorian homeschooling comes up.
162: The Melbourne Grand Prix drew 445,000 people through the gates in 2023, yet Jase finds it still leans on government money. He goes through the numbers: $230 million in revenue against $265 million in expenses, the state contribution, and the Australian Grand Prix Act of 1994. The hosts also cover how Drive to Survive changed the sport's audience, what drivers are paid and Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari deal.
163: Daniel Breese went from playing AFL for the Melbourne Demons to founding a retail business and now heading up growth at the offshoring company AS White Global. He joins Nick and Jase to explain how offshoring has moved beyond junior admin work to mid level qualified roles, why strengths differ by country, whether it only suits big businesses, and how provider models handle employment and HR.
164: Would you really end up a million dollars better off by investing in an index fund instead of paying down the home loan? Jase brings an article on that idea, with a 9.8% historic return and $200 a week as the example, and the hosts test it. They talk about capital gains tax on investments versus a family home, living off dividends, offset accounts, the higher concessional super limit of $30K, and the comfort some people get from being debt-free.
165: Victoria's debt is the target of Marty's frustration this week. He points to state debt heading from $55.2 billion in 2019 to $247 billion, and the hosts ask why capable people avoid politics, what population growth does to roads and transport, why a $1.1 billion prison near Geelong sits empty, and what the suburban rail loop has cost so far.
166: What is trade finance, and why do so many business owners not know about it? Nick, Jase and Marty explain how it bridges the gap between paying suppliers and getting paid, especially for importers, exporters, manufacturers and e-commerce businesses, including paying overseas suppliers in advance and funding against invoices. Nick also raises his concern about fast digital lending without advice and why matching the product to the need matters.
167: Property prices are starting to climb again even though interest rates have stopped rising, and the hosts dig into why. They cover how different lenders can change what someone can borrow, housing affordability and the supply shortage, build to rent, Jase's property regret, and ideas like modular homes and room by room renting, where Marty hears of 2,500 rooms available against 12,500 flatmates looking.
168: How do you put a number on a billionaire? Jase unpacks how the 250 rich list is put together, from adding up assets and subtracting liabilities to the trouble of valuing private companies, and why some listed names may be paper billionaires rather than cashed up. The hosts also discuss tech and crypto wealth, tall poppy syndrome in Australia, and what billionaires contribute through jobs and taxes.
169: Can a board game teach a kid more about money than a lecture? Nick brings Robert Kiyosaki's Cashflow, with its rat race and fast track, and Jase and Marty add Monopoly, chess and Life from their own families. They talk about how games build financial intelligence and strategic thinking, then land on four plain business questions from a story about Kerry Packer: who do we owe, who owes us, how much is in the bank, and did we make money this month.
170: Hiring is a big investment, so Marty walks through the checklist he has built over 25 years. He covers interview red flags such as blaming market conditions or other people, why a couple of years in a previous role signals loyalty, and how grading candidates out of 10 sharpens gut feel. The hosts also talk about setting clear expectations, onboarding, probation, and the hard call of letting someone go.
171: Small businesses are feeling the squeeze as the ATO collects. Jase, Nick and Marty talk about the roughly $50 billion owed by Victorian businesses, why payment plans now need far more information, and Marty's statistic that only 42% of small businesses are profitable. Jase explains the small business restructure as a gentler option than liquidation, and they cover which money is not yours to spend and why lodging on time still matters.
172: What does a three hour live event teach a podcaster about small details? Jase reports back from Steven Bartlett's speaking tour, where Steven asked for the name of the podcast and talked about things like room temperature and oxygen in a studio. The hosts turn that into talk about sweating the small stuff, treating failure as feedback, the Microsoft CEO laughing at the iPhone, and what AI might mean for content.
173: Paying wages, super or the ATO by card can give a business 30 or 60 days of breathing room and earn rewards along the way. Grant Austin explains how pay.com.au handles business payments, linked to Xero or bank files, without needing an Amex of your own. He covers moving from Chartered Accountant to founder, choosing which projects move the needle during fast growth, partnerships with big brands, investors and the importance of an exit plan.
174: How do you lead when you know how you like to be led? The hosts talk about authentic leadership and the idea of a human advisory board, the people you draw lessons from. Marty, Nick and Jase each name leaders they admire, from Federer to an NBA coach, and discuss clarity, autonomy and accountability when managing a team.
175: Do you need to be wealthy to see a financial planner? Senior financial planner Luke Mase says the bulk of his clients are ordinary mums and dads. He joins Nick and Marty to talk about super and risk profiles, what the conversation looks like for someone close to retirement, why insurance such as income protection belongs in a plan, and how the age pension fits in.
176: Nick had only ever seen Bonza's advertising on the side of a plane, and that is part of why the hosts think the airline struggled. They look at the app-only booking that kept it off comparison sites, the regional niche it chose, why running just 4 planes left little room to grow, and how hard Australia is for a new airline to crack. Jase also shares his London Marathon trip and a lost bag in Dubai.
177: Denmark gets 81% of its energy from renewables while Australia sits at 32%, a gap Jase noticed on a UK trip after the London marathon, where wind turbines, electric cars and street charging poles were everywhere. The hosts ask why Australia leans so heavily on coal, gas and mining, how incentives and culture shape behaviour, and what the path forward in green energy could look like.
178: What keeps a daily habit alive for more than 1300 days? Greg Bramich tells Jase and Marty how a mate's challenge turned into a running streak, the near miss around day 700 when he was sick, and how coaching, recovery and a goal of the six marathon majors before he turns 40 keep him improving. They link it back to business, with discipline, support from others and a simple answer to excuses: why not?
179: What does waiting for the right time cost? Marty crunches the numbers on a decade of property growth across the capitals, including 96.8% in Brisbane and 82.3% in Adelaide, against far slower wage growth. He shows how an $80,000 income and an $800,000 loan squeeze the budget, why the wealth gap keeps widening, and Jase shares his own story of getting the timing wrong. Where to find help for financial and mental health stress gets a mention too.
180: Why would Warren Buffett trim Apple and buy into insurance giant Chubb? Nick explains the insurance float, which across four insurance holdings gives Berkshire Hathaway around $164 billion to invest, and why a move toward financial products fits a time when people are doing it tough. The hosts then bring the idea down to small business, asking whether spare cash sitting in a trading account is working, and look at DR Horton.
181: Payroll tax thresholds, rising WorkCover premiums, super paid late and HELP debt changes are some of the areas Jase walks business owners through ahead of tax time. He explains why a forecast helps catch a payroll tax bill, the move to payday super in 2026, family trusts and capital gains tax, how a super contribution can reduce taxable income, and what happens when you sell a fully written off asset.
182: Is Gen Z entitled, or just clear about what they want? Marty brings the question, describing people born between 1997 and 2012 as tech savvy, innovative and focused on outcomes, while Nick wonders whether an easier upbringing shapes expectations. The hosts discuss setting clear metrics, letting people find their own route to results, mental health, hybrid work and environmental policies, and what employers risk if they ignore the next generation.
183: Could you secure a property with as little as $10,000 down? Coposit, a new product, lets buyers put down a smaller amount now and save the rest of the deposit while an off the plan property is built. Marty explains how it works using a $750,000 purchase with a 10% deposit of $75,000, why developers need presales, that there is no interest, and how CBA treats the deposit. The hosts also look at property share products.
184: A video on the cost of living in Australia struck a nerve on Instagram, so the show's producer reads out the top comments and Marty and Nick respond. They work through the blame placed on government policy, big corporations and immigration, the argument that people need to live within their means, and what rising minimum wage and super costs mean for small business owners competing against the supermarkets.
185: Marty's ten year old son Charlie has been picking up his dad's investing habits and has now researched a share of his own. Marty walks Nick and Producer Tommy through how Charlie scored a US home builder on revenue and profit growth, fair value, financial discipline and future opportunity. They also cover why business owners can make good investors, what an ETF is, and how parents can start these conversations. The hosts stress it is not financial advice.
186: A stolen bag in December turned into identity fraud by Christmas Day, and producer Tommy shares what followed: a patchy reporting process, hoops to jump through with the bank, changing the house keys and finding IDCARE. He and the hosts explain how a credit block through Equifax works, what thieves can do with a stolen licence, and ways to protect personal information, including app versus SMS two factor authentication.
187: The stage 3 tax cuts work out to an average of about $1,889 a year, or around $36 a week, which does not sound like much. The hosts show what that small amount can do, from compounding at 8 percent into $27,197 over 10 years to extra mortgage repayments, credit card interest, HELP debt indexation and salary sacrificing into super. Jase, Nick and Marty talk through the options rather than letting it vanish into everyday spending.
188: Is luck random, or something you can influence? The hosts split it into young luck, skill luck, performance luck, team luck and partnership luck, with Jase retracing how a police fitness test and his McDonald's years shaped his path into accounting. Marty puts luck at 90 percent controllable, Nick sees breaks as the reward for work done beforehand, and they cover why knowledge without action goes nowhere and why top teams don't carry weak performers.
189: Victoria has a long list of property taxes, and some landlords are selling up. Nick asks whether contrarian thinking points back to Melbourne, and the hosts cover land tax, windfall gains and the absentee owner surcharge, an AFR landlord who said he had four debts instead of four assets, and why fewer landlords means rising rents. They compare Melbourne with Perth, Sydney and Queensland, and note it is tipped to be Australia's biggest city by 2034.
190: How do you cut through when everyone is competing for attention? Using Mr Beast as the starting point, from a handful of followers early on to over 151 million subscribers at 25, the hosts ask what a small business can borrow from his marketing. They talk about consistency, engaging an audience, having a marketing plan, measuring return, presentations, and Marty's habit of buying coffees to introduce himself locally.
191: Buying a job and buying a business are two different things, and the hosts start by asking whether you're really ready for the second. Nick says banks have more appetite to finance quality established businesses and like buyers to have skin in the game, while property as security can sometimes stretch terms to 15 to 30 years. They also cover cash flow forecasts that can carry the loan repayments, acquisitions as a way to add revenue overnight, and due diligence.
192: Apple's move into buy now, pay later raises a bigger question for the hosts: what does easy credit do to spending habits and financial literacy, especially for young people with a phone in hand? They talk about financing cars, how lay by taught budgeting discipline, and why cash builds better habits. Nick also shares that smartphone transactions in Australia reached $93 billion in 2022, with 15.3 million cards registered to iPhones.
193: Clementine Boshevski grew Salt Lab from a bottle of magnesium handed to gym members, after seeing deficiency firsthand and living through her own burnout. She tells Jase and Marty how she funded her first gym on credit cards, why founder-led content worked, what magnesium does, how she handled supplier terms and cash flow, and how she kept going after a warehouse fire destroyed $1.5 million of stock.
194: A question from a YouTube viewer sets up this walk through of bucket companies. Jase explains why profit that is not needed personally can be taxed at 25 or 30 cents in the dollar instead of 47 cents, runs a worked example with a sole trader called Dave, and covers the common misconception that the money must actually move into the company.
