Marty and Tommy ask about the tax can being kicked down the road, protecting assets and investing inside the company.
195: Is anxiety a normal part of running a business, or a signal that something needs to change? Marty and Jase, joined by producer Tommy, share personal experiences of work stress, from deadlines and ATO pressure to the loop between exercise and sleep. They talk about recognising triggers, taking criticism without getting defensive, daily rituals and self-care, and knowing when to build your capacity versus change your situation.
196: Australian retirees are reported to be sitting on $1.3 trillion of equity in their own homes, so where does property fit into retirement planning? Nick, Jase and Marty look at being asset rich and cash poor, the three things to build wealth around, and why the family home is usually the one that gets sold. They also cover the tax risk of claiming part of your home as a work space, guarantor loans for kids and grandkids, and downsizer contributions into super.
197: How do you set a business up for a new financial year? The hosts cover planning days and sharing the vision with staff, why a budget needs a monthly review because you can't turn a ship around quickly, and a mail automation example that cuts 30,000 pieces of mail down to about 20 documents a week for a person to check. Google reviews, customer surveys, compliance and getting finance advice early round it out.
198: When banks say no, private credit says maybe, and the hosts look at why it is growing. Marty cites a 16% year on year rise in private lending and explains how it can help fund the purchase of a business with equity behind it, why lenders charge more than banks, and how quickly it can be arranged. Along the way they discuss recession worries, rate cuts, the need for a clear exit strategy and speaking to professionals first.
199: Why does a bank test your home loan at a rate higher than the one you pay? Nick explains APRA's 3% serviceability buffer, the noise around lowering it, and why he thinks caution reflects economic uncertainty and mortgage arrears. He also shows how the stage 3 tax cuts lift borrowing power, with a single person able to borrow $642,000 after the cuts, $27,000 more than before, and looks at non-bank lenders.
201: Plenty of costly tax mistakes come down to records. Jase goes through where people trip up: home office claims that need a diary of hours worked from home, bank statements standing in for receipts, car claims without a logbook, rental property deductions, and income that does not match what the ATO already holds, including crypto. The hosts also cover the Medicare levy and surcharge, and what audit insurance is.
202: Landlords and tenants are both under strain. Marty, Jase and Nick compare an investor's numbers from 2021 with today, where a property that left an investor about $5,000 in the green now costs about $22,000 out of pocket. They also cover how competitive renting has become, how negative gearing softens the blow, why some investors sell even when they can afford to hold, and what holding a property involves.
203: If you could start your business again today, what would you do differently? Jase, Nick and Marty look back at their early days and weigh them against what they'd do now, from a basic business plan and getting on top of GST and reporting sooner, to proving the concept and cash flow before spending on infrastructure and branding. They also cover digital marketing, finding your ideal customer, referrals and the value of a mentor.
204: Jase says the only reason he does not react to market swings is that he forgot his share trading login. Nick uses the volatility to explain asset allocation, the split between defensive and growth assets, and why a risk profile that suits your stage of life helps in a crash. He covers rebalancing with a worked example, a balanced profile for retirees, and the cost of selling after a fall and then sitting out the recovery.
205: Who is setting up self managed super funds these days? Marty cites established members at a median age of 62, newly established members averaging 46, and the 35 to 44 group now making up 10% of members. The hosts cover individual versus corporate trustees, why a statement of advice matters, borrowing through bare trusts, buying property inside a fund, and how lenders approach SMSF loans and refinancing.
206: Why do so many owners build a business and end up with the life they were trying to avoid? Adam Diamond talks with Nick and Jase about working on the business rather than only in it, making reporting and consistency a habit, and why a first hire who costs more than you pay yourself can still make sense. He also covers accountability, implementing the advice you pay for, and giving clear direction.
207: Why is one cafe lined up out the door while the one next door sits empty? That question drives a talk about points of difference. The hosts discuss how customers who can't tell you from a competitor choose on price, why basics like efficiency and good service get forgotten in a boom, how a surprise Sunday phone call won Marty over as a customer, and why asking happy clients for referrals works.
208: Should first home buyers be able to use their super for a deposit? Nick brings a proposal heading to a Senate inquiry, and the hosts argue it out: the political motives, the fact investors can already tap super for property, what early withdrawal could mean at retirement, and whether the real fix is housing supply. Nick also explains why a family home does little for retirement unless it is sold.
209: When did you last step out of your business for some training? Jase shares what he took from a three day course on strategy, starting with defining your ideal business through purpose, vision and values, then looking honestly at your current situation. The hosts discuss getting clarity, why mentors and advisors matter, what they would do with an extra hour every day for a year, and what a SWOT has shown their own business.
210: Property listings are up around 10% and Marty says activity is picking up, so the hosts ask what it takes to be ready when the right place appears. Marty explains why a rough idea of borrowing power is not enough, why lenders differ on what you can afford, and why knowing your maximum helps you stay confident with an offer. Nick adds that nearly everyone feels they overspent, and Jase compares pre-approval to laying out your running gear.
211: Financial wellbeing is about more than being wealthy. Nick leads the others through what it means, with Jase calling it feeling comfortable and Marty describing a plan he believes in. They cover savings for financial shocks, why budgets and mapped out steps matter, the stages from turmoil through to flourishing, a financial wellbeing score, and why knowing your numbers is where it starts.
212: The show's producer has just come back from more than a month on the road in the US filming a documentary on American gun culture, driving from California to Florida during the election buildup. He shares what he saw with Jase and Marty, and then they ask what a second Trump term could mean for Australia, from business and tariffs to US debt, inflation and interest rates.
213: Knowledge is power, but maybe not so much anymore, says Marty, now that anyone can access it, so the question becomes how you use it. That leads to being AI-curious rather than an AI expert, with Jase and Producer Tommy sharing how AI tools bring efficiencies to their work. The conversation also covers Adrian Portelli's house giveaway and its capital gains questions, what pushed Tommy to start his own business, and healthy profit margins.
214: In the 1950s the global fertility rate was around five children per woman, and Australia's is now 1.66. With Nick back after becoming a new dad, the hosts talk about what parenthood has surprised him with, why birth rates are falling, how childcare and housing costs weigh on families, and the private versus public schooling debate. They also touch on what financial planning covers for parents.
215: December and January can squeeze a business's cash even when the year has gone well. Marty shares a tight patch that followed heavy investment in his team, and the hosts look at research showing nearly 18 percent of small business owners have no cash reserves, plus talk of the harshest conditions since the GFC. They cover planning around the peaks and troughs of your own year, short term funding such as overdrafts, and speaking with an accountant or broker first.
216: Do vision boards actually work? Marty admits he once thought they were rubbish, until goals he had put on a laptop screensaver and forgotten were all accomplished five years later. Nick prefers strategy and struggles with long-term visions because things change so fast, and Jase looks back at his own board, including paid keynote speaking. The hosts also share the Jim Carrey cheque story and why feeling fulfilled today matters.
217: The hosts look back at what they predicted for 2024 and forward to 2025. Jase's call that AI would become more embedded in everyday life held up, as did Nick's call on Donald Trump's return to office. The new predictions cover AI agents, virtual reality meetings, robot sport, GST and Melbourne property, where Marty forecasts a 14 to 15% rise in values once the fear of missing out kicks in.
219: Is residential property still the way to passive income, or does commercial do it better? Nick shares a couple who built an $8M portfolio, then realised houses would not reach the $300,000 of passive income they wanted and moved towards commercial. The hosts weigh pros and cons of each, including a $1.5 million comparison showing a $53,000 cash flow difference, and risks like longer periods with no rent.
221: Could a can of water teach a finance firm how to stand out? The hosts look at Liquid Death, worth $1.4 billion by Marty's figures, and its aggressive branding, aluminium cans and playful lines like hydrate or die. They compare Red Bull and Monster's extreme sport marketing, giving product away at events and making content people actually share, then ask how service businesses like accounting and mortgage broking can find a point of difference, such as a social mission.
224: Are you a hunter or a farmer when it comes to sales? Marty draws on over 30 years in leadership to explain that hunters chase new deals while farmers grow existing clients through service and referrals, and the hosts place themselves on that scale. They look at accounting, financial planning and mortgage broking, why sales hires fail when the role is wrong, and whether a hunter can be trained to farm.
234: Tax planning sounds boring, but Jase argues it's one of the most crucial things a business owner can do. With Nick and Marty, he covers how to work out which cash in the business account is really yours, why trust distributions need sorting before 30 June, how tighter ATO data matching changes things, what goes wrong with company loans, and what an accountant looks at in a tax planning meeting.
236: What happens when you build a property portfolio too fast and lose it all before you are 25? Chris Christofi, CEO of Reventon, tells Nick and Jase how he went from $348,000 in debt to over $3.2 billion in property sales and 3,400+ clients. He talks about selling scratch tickets at age 10, learning from elite athletes, why a divorce forced a reset, and raising over $1M through the Vinnies CEO Sleepout and his Lead With Kindness campaign.
243: Why can a cheese shop be more profitable than a builder? Marty and the hosts explain gross versus net profit with a plumbing example, show how a higher gross margin leaves room to move when costs climb, and unpack why construction's slim margins and high insolvency numbers leave little room for error. A $3 million contract expected to return $150,000 shows how a bad contract bites, alongside smart tweaks to a business model.
248: Why do Australians favour property over shares, and what do the numbers say over 20 years? Nick compares a result of $1.365 million for property with $1.335 million for shares, and looks at what holding a Victorian rental can drain from weekly cashflow, around $470 a week in his example. The hosts also cover liquidity, stamp duty, the emotional strength shares demand, Marty's changing view, and new rental laws.
252: Is the country's biggest property portal too powerful? REA Group draws over 12 million users a month, agents face subscription fee hikes, and the ACCC is asking questions about postcode pricing. The hosts unpack how the network effect built its lead over Domain, now backed by an American owner, whether any competitor can break through, and whether other businesses could build a network effect of their own.
253: Marty lost money on a leveraged investment during the GFC, Nick has had speculative micro caps go to zero, and Jase sank money into a Geelong commercial property that did not go to plan. From those mistakes the hosts discuss dollar cost averaging, how few stocks drive market returns, stop losses, Buffett holding cash and how often markets fall, plus what a high market PE has meant for the next decade of returns.
